title: Respiratory syncytial virus incidence and clinical outcomes in patients with inflammatory bowel disease: a National Veterans Affairs cohort study.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Data describing the incidence and clinical outcomes of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection among patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) are limited.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We conducted a nationwide retrospective cohort study using the Veterans Health Administration (VHA) database. Adults with IBD were identified using a previously validated algorithm and matched 1:2 to non-IBD controls using propensity score matching. Laboratory-confirmed RSV infections that occurred between January 1, 2021, and December 31, 2024, were identified using standardized laboratory codes and confirmed by manual chart adjudication.
analysis.methods: Primary outcomes included RSV incidence and hospitalizations. Secondary outcomes included intensive care unit (ICU) admission and patient outcomes stratified by IBD medication class.
analysis.main_results: After propensity score matching, 52 740 IBD patients and 104 997 non-IBD controls were included. Infection with RSV occurred in 219 patients with IBD and 426 non-IBD patients. Incidence rates of RSV were similar between cohorts across all years in our study period. Hospitalization related to RSV occurred in 18.26% of IBD-RSV patients compared with 13.15% of non-IBD patients (P = .08). ICU admission was rare in both groups (<1%).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: In this nationwide cohort, patients with IBD, with predominantly lower exposure to advanced therapies, did not have higher rates of RSV infection or worse clinical outcomes compared with matched non-IBD controls. RSV outcomes were similar across IBD medication classes.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings support current vaccination recommendations and provide reassurance regarding RSV risk among patients with IBD.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report specific limitations of the study design.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to investigate the incidence and clinical outcomes of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection among patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). A nationwide retrospective cohort study was conducted using the Veterans Health Administration (VHA) database, where adults with IBD were matched 1:2 to non-IBD controls. The study identified RSV infections between 2021 and 2024 and assessed outcomes such as hospitalization and ICU admission. Results showed similar RSV incidence rates between IBD and non-IBD patients, with no significant difference in hospitalization rates. The findings suggest that IBD patients do not have higher RSV infection rates or worse clinical outcomes compared to non-IBD controls, and outcomes were consistent across different IBD medication classes. These results support existing vaccination recommendations and offer reassurance about RSV risk in IBD patients. The study's evidence is strong, but specific limitations were not detailed.

title: Circulating Biomarkers Associated with Severe Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infection in Infants Under 2 Years: A Systematic Review

analysis.scope_and_question: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of acute lower respiratory tract infection in infants, but circulating biomarkers for severity stratification remain insufficiently validated.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: This systematic review evaluated circulating biomarkers associated with acute RSV disease severity in children aged ≤ 24 months. PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched for English-language reports published between 1 January 2016 and 1 March 2026, with the last searches performed on 1 March 2026. Study-level risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale or the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist, according to study design.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Findings were synthesized descriptively using study-level effect estimates and reported severity-discrimination measures. In one cohort, fibrinogen and the fibrinogen-to-albumin ratio (FAR) showed large differences between severity groups; FAR had a reported AUC of 0.875.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Biomarker associations varied across populations, age strata, sampling times, and severity definitions, and reproducibility across independent cohorts was limited. Important limitations include heterogeneous clinical comparisons, limited confounder adjustment, and predominantly single-cohort evidence. These findings do not establish comparative superiority or external validity.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Whether these markers add useful information to clinical assessment requires prospective validation. Current evidence does not support using FAR, the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), or other circulating biomarkers alone to predict subsequent clinical deterioration.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review investigates circulating biomarkers associated with severe respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection in infants under 2 years. The review included 24 studies contributing 174 extractable comparisons, with evidence sourced from PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus between 2016 and 2026. title: Diagnostic performance of antigen-based rapid test kits for six respiratory viruses in children: comparison with a multiplex PCR panel and correlation with viral load.

Specimens positive by either method underwent confirmatory quantitative real-time PCR to determine viral load.

This highlights the utility of antigen testing in identifying children with the highest viral burden.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results clarify the clinical role of rapid antigen testing for RSV, showing its reliability in detecting high viral load cases, which are most likely to represent acute, symptomatic infection requiring immediate clinical action.

The study was conducted at a pediatric center, where two simultaneous nasopharyngeal swabs were collected from 1,232 children. For RSV, antigen test positivity increased steeply with viral load, approaching 90–100% at loads ≥10^6–10^7 copies/100 μL. These findings support the use of antigen testing to identify children with the highest viral burden, who are most likely to have acute infection. title: Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infection in Children During the COVID-19 Pandemic: Findings from a Tertiary-Care Pediatric Cohort

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a major cause of lower respiratory tract infection in children. This study aimed to describe the clinical and laboratory characteristics of RSV-positive children older than 28 days in a tertiary-care cohort, explore characteristics associated with hospitalization in group comparisons, and identify factors independently associated with pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) admission among hospitalized children.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This retrospective single-center study screened RSV testing records between August 2020 and August 2022 and included children older than 28 days with laboratory-confirmed RSV infection identified between February 2021 and August 2022. Of the 3523 children with available RSV test results during the study period, 561 RSV-positive children aged >28 days were included.
analysis.methods: Demographic, clinical, laboratory, treatment, hospitalization, PICU admission, respiratory support, and outcome data were recorded. Comparisons were performed according to hospitalization status, clinical diagnosis, and PICU admission. A prespecified parsimonious multivariable logistic regression model evaluated factors associated with PICU admission among hospitalized children.
analysis.main_results: Hospitalization was required in 478 patients (85.2%), and 35 (6.2%) required PICU admission. Pneumonia was associated with higher rates of hypoxia, noninvasive ventilatory support, PICU admission, longer hospitalization, and delayed clinical improvement. Documented viral coinfection was detected in 30 patients (5.3%); no association was detected between documented viral coinfections and hospitalizations or PICU admission in this dataset.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Pneumonia and hypoxia were independently associated with PICU admission in this tertiary-care cohort. The study highlights the clinical features and risk factors for PICU admission in RSV-infected children, providing insights into the severity of RSV disease.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform surveillance and risk assessment strategies for RSV in pediatric populations, particularly in identifying high-risk patients who may require intensive care. They also support the development of targeted interventions for managing severe RSV infections.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and single-center setting, which may affect generalizability. The evidence is moderate as it is based on a tertiary-care cohort and does not include prospective data or external validation.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the clinical and laboratory characteristics of RSV-positive children during the COVID-19 pandemic, focusing on factors associated with hospitalization and PICU admission. It found that pneumonia and hypoxia were independently linked to PICU admission, while viral coinfections were not associated with increased hospitalization or PICU admission. The study highlights the importance of monitoring severe RSV cases in pediatric populations, particularly those with pneumonia or hypoxia, to improve clinical management and resource allocation. However, its retrospective design and single-center setting limit the generalizability of the findings, resulting in moderate confidence in the conclusions.

title: RSV Bivalent Prefusion F Protein Vaccine in Pregnancy and Protection Against RSV-Associated Illness in Infants: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on the effectiveness of the RSV bivalent prefusion F protein vaccine (RSVpreF) administered during pregnancy in preventing RSV-associated lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) in infants. The central question is whether RSVpreF provides protection against RSV-related illness in infants, with a specific emphasis on hospitalization due to LRTI.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review conducted a systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, and Europe PMC from January 1, 2020, through January 30, 2026. A total of 1144 studies were initially identified, and all were screened independently by 2 reviewers. The meta-analysis used random-effects models with Hartung-Knapp adjustment and Sidik-Jonkman estimator to pool odds ratios (ORs). Vaccine effectiveness was calculated as (1 - OR) × 100% for the primary outcome of RSV-associated LRTI hospitalization.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The pooled vaccine effectiveness against RSV-associated LRTI hospitalization was 82% (95% CI, 81%-82%) in infants from birth to 3 months and 78% (95% CI, 70%-84%) in infants from birth to 6 months, when mothers were vaccinated 14 days or more before delivery. These results support the effectiveness of RSVpreF in pregnancy for preventing RSV-associated LRTI hospitalization during the first 6 months of life.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The limited available data precluded meta-analysis of effectiveness against secondary outcomes such as RSV-associated emergency department visits, intensive care unit admissions, and death. This indicates a gap in the evidence for these specific outcomes, which are not fully addressed in the current review.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The results support the introduction of RSVpreF into routine antenatal immunization programs. Further research is needed to evaluate its effectiveness against secondary outcomes and to expand the geographic and demographic scope of the studies.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluates the effectiveness of the RSV bivalent prefusion F protein vaccine (RSVpreF) administered during pregnancy in preventing RSV-associated lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) in infants. The review synthesized real-world evidence from 7 studies involving 7112 infants, with 2684 born to vaccinated mothers. Pooled vaccine effectiveness against RSV-associated LRTI hospitalization was 82% (95% CI, 81%-82%) in infants from birth to 3 months and 78% (95% CI, 70%-84%) in infants from birth to 6 months, when mothers were vaccinated 14 days or more before delivery. These findings support the use of RSVpreF in antenatal immunization programs. However, the limited data precluded meta-analysis of secondary outcomes such as emergency department visits, ICU admissions, and mortality. The review highlights the need for further research to address these gaps and to confirm the vaccine's broader impact on RSV-related illnesses in infants.

title: RSV Disease Burden in Adults in Emerging Market Countries, a Systematic Review and Modelling Analysis

analysis.scope_and_question: Abstract Background Most previous studies on adult respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) burden focus on high-income settings (HIC).
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: Methods We conducted a systematic review (PROSEPRO: CRD420251137828) to identify studies reporting estimates of RSV burden from any care setting in adults>18 years in EMC.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Findings We included 70 studies of which the majority were from China (30/70) and PCR was the predominant diagnostic method (59/70). Adjusted RSV disease incidence rate (approximately 2.5 times higher than unadjusted) ranged from 2,544 (95% CI 1,352-4,787) per 100,000 in adults aged 18-49 years to 2,392 (1,618-3,534) in adults ≥65 years after accounting for clinical sampling and diagnostic testing. Adjusted hospitalisation rates increased with age, from 20 (8-51) per 100,000 in 18-49 years to 74 (3-2,027) in adults ≥65 years, representing an approximate 2.5-fold increase after adjustment. The adjusted RSV proportion positive was relatively stable, ranging from 1.8% (0.4-8.5) to 9.7% (6.3-14.6), regardless of settings or clinical case definitions.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The unadjusted in-hospital case fatality ratio (hCFR) was 6.0% (2.9-11.9) in adults ≥65 years vs 3.1 (2.0-5.0) in those 18-49 years. In-hospital CFR are comparable to or higher than in HIC.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: With the recent approval of RSV vaccines for adults, extending epidemiological understanding to emerging market countries (EMC) is critical for informing prevention strategies.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review and modelling analysis aimed to characterize the burden of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) among adults ≥18 years in emerging market countries (EMC). The review included 70 studies, predominantly from China, using PCR as the main diagnostic method. Adjusted RSV incidence rates were found to be 2,544 (95% CI 1,352-4,787) per 100,000 in adults aged 18-49 years and 2,392 (1,618-3,534) in adults ≥65 years. Adjusted hospitalisation rates increased with age, from 20 (8-51) per 100,000 in 18-49 years to 74 (3-2,027) in adults ≥65 years. The adjusted proportion positive of RSV was relatively stable, ranging from 1.8% (0.4-8.5) to 9.7% (6.3-14.6). The unadjusted in-hospital case fatality ratio (hCFR) was 6.0% (2.9-11.9) in adults ≥65 years versus 3.1% (2.0-5.0) in those aged 18-49 years. The study concluded that RSV disease burden in EMC is substantially lower than in high-income settings (HIC). The authors suggested that narrow case definitions, less sensitive testing, reduced healthcare access, and incomplete surveillance may contribute to these lower estimates. The findings highlight the importance of extending epidemiological understanding to EMC to inform RSV prevention strategies, especially with the recent approval of RSV vaccines for adults.

title: Shifting viral aetiology, codetection and age-specific mortality in severe acute respiratory infection in Brazil, 2022-2025: a nationwide surveillance study.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory viral aetiology and codetection among severe acute respiratory infection (SARI) notifications have evolved post-COVID-19.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The supplied evidence does not report study design or population details.
analysis.methods: We analysed nationwide SIVEP-Gripe SARI records (2022-2025; extracted July 2026) with RT-PCR viral detection.
analysis.main_results: Among 447,107 virus-positive records, 7.2% involved codetections and 25.4% included RSV. Isolated SARS-CoV-2 declined from 72.4% (2022) to 6.8% (2025), while codetections rose from 3.0% to 11.2%. Compared to isolated RSV, mortality was higher for codetection without RSV (aRR 1.80, 95% CI: 1.67-1.94), isolated SARS-CoV-2 (1.62, 1.54-1.70), and codetection with RSV (1.40, 1.27-1.55). Associations varied by age ($p < .001$). Among RSV-positive cases, codetection conferred increased mortality risk (aRR 1.46, 1.32-1.61). Excluding isolated SARS-CoV-2 attenuated the 2025-versus-2022 codetection prevalence ratio from 1.85 to 1.10.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Viral detections shifted towards greater heterogeneity, strongly driven by changing surveillance composition.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Integrated, age-sensitive surveillance with standardized diagnostic reporting is essential; surveillance proportions do not reflect population incidence.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: We examined temporal patterns, age heterogeneity, and severe outcome associations in Brazil.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the evolving viral aetiology and codetection patterns in severe acute respiratory infection (SARI) notifications in Brazil from 2022 to 2025. It highlights the shift in viral detection towards greater heterogeneity, driven by changes in surveillance composition. The findings reveal that codetection with RSV and other viruses is associated with increased mortality risk compared to isolated RSV cases. The study underscores the importance of integrated, age-sensitive surveillance with standardized diagnostic reporting to accurately reflect population incidence. However, the study's limitations include the reliance on surveillance data, which may not capture true population trends due to varying testing indications and panels. The evidence suggests a moderate confidence level in the findings due to the observational nature of the study and potential biases in surveillance data.

title: Non-invasive quantification of lower airway antigen-specific antibodies using exhaled breath particles - an observational proof-of-concept study.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Advancements in mucosal vaccine development highlight the urgent need for practical methods to assess immune responses in both upper and lower airways.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We used Particles in Exhaled Air (PExA), a non-invasive method capturing aerosolised respiratory tract lining fluid (RTLF) from the distal airways, to quantify antigen-specific IgA and IgG. Antibodies were measured in paired serum, nasal secretions, and PExA samples from 28 healthcare workers during spring 2025, including 18 with RT-qPCR-confirmed RSV infection.
analysis.methods: Antibodies were measured in paired serum, nasal secretions, and PExA samples from 28 healthcare workers during spring 2025, including 18 with RT-qPCR-confirmed SARS-CoV-2, influenza A (H1N1), or respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection.
analysis.main_results: Antigen-specific IgA and IgG measurements in PExA samples showed low variability (median CVs: spike-IgA 3.7%, H1-IgA 7.2%, RSV pre-F-IgA 5.3%). Strong correlations (Spearman's rho >0.85, p < 0.0001) were observed between PExA and serum IgG, which may be consistent with a systemic contribution to lower-airway IgG levels. In contrast, IgA correlations were more modest, which may reflect local IgA production in the lungs.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: This study demonstrates the feasibility of non-invasive measurement of antigen-specific antibodies in the lower airways. Our approach proposes a framework for assessing lower-airway immunity and supporting next-generation mucosal vaccine development.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide a non-invasive method for assessing lower-airway immunity, which could inform surveillance, diagnosis, and vaccine development for respiratory syncytial virus infection.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to a small sample size and observational design, but the results are consistent with expected isotype distribution in upper and lower airways, suggesting moderate evidence strength.

analysis.summary_en: This observational proof-of-concept study explores the feasibility of non-invasive quantification of antigen-specific antibodies in the lower airways using exhaled breath particles (PExA). The research highlights the need for practical methods to assess immune responses in both upper and lower airways, particularly for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection. The study measured IgA and IgG in paired serum, nasal secretions, and PExA samples from 28 healthcare workers, including 18 with RT-qPCR-confirmed RSV infection. Results showed low variability in PExA measurements and strong correlations with serum IgG, suggesting systemic contributions to lower-airway IgG levels. In contrast, IgA correlations were more modest, possibly reflecting local production in the lungs. The findings demonstrate the potential of PExA as a tool for assessing lower-airway immunity and supporting mucosal vaccine development. However, the study's small sample size and observational nature limit its generalisability, resulting in moderate evidence strength.

title: Upper Airway and Neurological Manifestations of Pediatric Omicron Infection: From Novel Pathogen to Endemic Respiratory Virus — A Natural Experiment in Immuno-naive versus Primed Children

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to characterize upper airway obstruction (UAO) and neurological events in hospitalized children with Omicron infection, to compare outcomes with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and human rhinovirus (HRV) using propensity score-matched analyzes, and to leverage a unique natural experiment to assess the impact of first versus second immune exposure on disease severity.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This retrospective cohort study identified 2,085 hospitalized children (0–18 years) with laboratory-confirmed infection: 211 with Omicron (temporal proxy), 424 with RSV, 824 with HRV, and 957 with other viruses. A natural-experiment analysis compared first exposure (Wave 1, December 2022–February 2023, n = 82) versus second exposure (Wave 2+, March–December 2023, n = 51) among children ≥ 6 months of age.
analysis.methods: Propensity score matching (1:2) compared Omicron with RSV and HRV, adjusting for age, sex, comorbidities, and admission severity. Age-stratified and wave-period analyzes were prespecified.
analysis.main_results: UAO occurred in 20 of 211 children with Omicron (9.5%, 95% CI 5.9–14.2%) versus 1 of 424 with RSV (0.2%) and 1 of 824 with HRV (0.2%). analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: After matching, Omicron was associated with increased risks of MODS score ≥ 2 (vs. RSV: RR 3.80, 95% CI 1.84–7.86; vs. HRV: RR 4.50, 95% CI 2.32–8.72), non-febrile neurological events (vs. RSV: RR 5.2, 95% CI 2.8–9.6; vs. HRV: RR 6.8, 95% CI 3.9–11.8), and severe adverse outcomes (vs. RSV: RR 3.08, 95% CI 1.52–6.24; vs. HRV: RR 3.85, 95% CI 1.98–7.49).
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings document the transition of Omicron from a novel, severe pediatric pathogen toward an established respiratory virus, and highlight the need for age-specific clinical vigilance and ongoing surveillance.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report limitations or evidence strength.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the clinical manifestations of pediatric Omicron infection, comparing it to RSV and HRV. It found that Omicron was associated with significantly higher rates of upper airway obstruction and neurological events than RSV or HRV. Propensity score matching revealed increased risks of severe outcomes with Omicron compared to these viruses. A natural experiment showed that immune priming reduced severe outcomes after second exposure. The findings suggest that Omicron has transitioned from a novel pathogen to an endemic respiratory virus, emphasizing the need for age-specific clinical monitoring. The study is limited by its retrospective design and the absence of detailed limitations or evidence strength assessment.

title: Prompt engineering for epidemiological surveillance: A step toward wider access to public health data analysis through natural language processing.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to describe and assess a framework that generates epidemiological analysis scripts from natural-language queries constrained by surveillance data dictionaries. analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved the development of a methodological framework with internal consistency assessment. Two authors with prior programming experience submitted identical sets of 22 in-scope and 22 scope-control queries across three case studies (respiratory syncytial virus, influenza A, and dengue) using Claude Opus 4.8 and Gemini 3.7 Flash against OpenDataSUS datasets.
analysis.methods: PEFES (Prompt Engineering for Epidemiological Surveillance) restricts large language model output to dictionary-declared variables and coding schemes, validates scope before generating a script, and does not execute code. The framework was tested by comparing generated scripts against predefined queries and datasets.
analysis.main_results: The two raters agreed on the behavior for all 22 scope-control queries: the 17 queries that were expected to be declined did not produce a script, and all 5 in-scope counterparts produced a script. The study highlights the potential of natural language processing in epidemiological surveillance.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: PEFES accelerates epidemiological work rather than replacing it, and it is a step toward wider access to surveillance data analysis. This could enhance the efficiency of public health data processing and interpretation.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Errors within the declared set were identified by rater review, not by the framework, motivating pre-execution type checks or returning unstated choices as clarification requests. The evidence is moderate as the study is based on internal consistency assessment and limited case studies.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduces PEFES, a framework that generates epidemiological analysis scripts from natural-language queries constrained by surveillance data dictionaries. The aim was to assess the framework's ability to restrict data analysis to dictionary-declared variables and coding schemes. Every source field read was dictionary-declared, and reported values were identical for 14 of the 22 in-scope queries. The framework's potential to accelerate epidemiological work and improve access to surveillance data analysis is highlighted, though the study's evidence is moderate due to its reliance on internal consistency assessment and limited case studies.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Induction of virus-specific immune responses in kidney transplant recipients (KTR) by vaccination is challenging.
